title: How to use pause reps for SIZE
summary: Explains pause reps as a hypertrophy tool: pausing until momentum dies reinforces technique, stability and confidence in the bottom 'red zone', adds stretched time under tension, and builds strength. Paused squat and bench are best; pauses are variations, not replacements for touch-and-go strength work, typically 3-4 sets of 4-12 reps 1-2x/week.
claims: Pause reps aren't just for powerlifters; bodybuilding should take any tool from any discipline that builds size
Bodybuilders need strength growth because it is the only way to grow tonnage at relevant intensity; pause reps build strength
For bodybuilding a pause rep has no fixed duration: you pause until momentum is killed, often about one second; competition-style pauses that heave back up don't count
Pausing removes momentum while keeping the stretch at the bottom, which is what you want

Pauses prevent form breakdown in the 'red zone' where the negative turns to positive (lost arch, shoulder drift, moving feet); breakdown leaks the kinetic chain and matters more in bodybuilding rep work than in single-rep powerlifting
The bottom of a squat should feel rock solid, like sitting; if it feels unstable that is a recipe for injury
Pauses add stretched time under tension, a small bonus rather than a major driver; don't do 20-second pauses
Lengthening work like paused squats and deadlifts helps prevent hamstring pulls, common in sprinters and soccer players who only train contraction
A technique you feel confident in is stronger; if your form feels rock solid it may be your strongest form even if observers disagree
His novice program squats twice a week, once regular and once paused; the paused squat is his exception to 'no variations for novices' because it is the safest squat and exposes technique errors
Pause squats remove fear of the hole and cure the yips; pause 1-2 seconds and don't rock or bounce before driving up
Pause reps force lighter weights and can't replace touch-and-go strength work; use them as variations
Bouncing the bench, dive-bombing squats or slamming deadlifts are ways of rushing through the feared bottom range, sacrificing tension, technique and joint health
Paused bench and paused squat are the best pause exercises; they tax the joints less, allowing more reps, volume and frequency
Paused deadlift: stop about an inch off the floor and hold, teaching rigidity and preventing hips shooting up; submaximal only; he skips it because the floor is his strong point
The deadlift builds the mid back better than the traps because of the back angle, and the paused deadlift extends that weighted stretch
If paused squats hurt your lower back, your squat form is bad; the pause exposes a compromised position you normally speed through
Paused bench eliminated his shoulder pain; he recommends it for anyone with pain on touch-and-go bench, and pec tear risk is minimal
Pauses on overhead press, curls, skullcrushers and pull-ups are less useful: no real technical or confidence benefit and many better variations exist
A paused skullcrusher maximizes the long-head stretch behind the head; paused pull-ups only work if the scapulae stay retracted at the bottom
Treat pause reps as variations complementing touch-and-go main lifts; as a main lift only in rotation (day A regular, day B paused); deadlifts are always from a dead stop
Use 3-4 sets of 6-10 or 8-12 reps; he stays at 6-8, sometimes 4, never below 4; above 12 is overkill
Paused squats and deadlifts tax the cardiovascular system, so paused deadlifts may need lower reps around 4
Don't open the day with pause work: slight fatigue keeps you from pushing into form breakdown
Pause work 1-2 times a week is fine, 3 is overkill; rotate within the line of specificity (squat with paused squat, not another lift)
exercises: bar dead on chest, then press; no heave
sit 1-2 s until momentum dies, no rocking
safest squat, cures fear of the hole
stop an inch off floor and hold, then finish
bar rests on body at bottom
pause at full stretch behind head
ok variation; dead hang disengages back
